doc.title: Mr. and Mrs. A.C. Synigal Interview, 1962-05-24

title: Alphonse Picou's funeral, heard about in the hospital
summary: Edna recalls Picou playing High Society at the Creole Fiesta and hearing from a nurse of his huge funeral while she was in hospital.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: Well, that was their way of doing it, I guess. They still do it. Well, they call it fun. What did they do at Pico's? I was in the hospital then.
They played, uh, oh, didn't he ramble the first number I believe before? Is that a picture on him? I don't know.
Well, he played the, you played the, didn't he ramble, yeah. Uh-huh.

You wouldn't tell me, because we should have sent him a floor. He played in the, uh, Creole Fiestas, um, concert. And there goes swag. He played that, uh, uh, Piccolo, Piccolo, Piccolo, huh? Well, he was the one, don't you remember? He played Piccolo, that, um, High Society? Oh, he, no one would play High Society like him. Oh, he played it that night like nobody did. And so, um, nobody told me about him. So, a nurse sneaked up in there and she said, Miss Senegal, did you know, um, Piccolo? I said, what Piccolo? Alphonse Piccolo, the, the band. He says, well, he got 50,000 people at his funeral this afternoon, this evening. I said, what, he's dead? I was in the hospital, too. Yeah, I remember, yeah. And I said,

my people not tell me, they think it's gonna affect me. I said, but, uh, Piccolo, that's not gonna affect me. And so, my daughter was here from California, and I asked her, Mama, don't be worried about that. You worry about getting yourself well, don't worry about the Piccolo, Piccolo. And so then, uh, we had a council with the nurses, and they all came around there, brought me some juices and everything. I said, let's talk about Piccolo. They said they had 50,000 people, at his funeral. I don't believe they had that many, though, huh? They said they had so many people.
They had lots of people on us. And White Acorns.
Everybody, second liners and everything. Second liners and everything. I heard about it last I came home, they told me all about it. I know his daughter.
It would've been hard to count. Huh? It would've been hard to count.
It was hard to tell what they were playing, too. There were so many people,
you could hardly hear the bomb. Yeah.

And Liz and Miles told me, she's strutting in the streets, too. She said, I and Ms. Menville. He said, Ms. Menville and her. You know Ms. Menville. Yes. Don't you? She and Ms. Menville had the streets for themselves. They were just strutting in the streets. I said, you mean, Liz, you all had that big time? I said, well, sure, we had a big time. They had to pick a, uh, something.
I'm sure that's what he wanted, too. Oh, he wanted. Oh, yeah.
I knew his daughter when she was a little girl. There's somebody right around the corner here. Right around the corner. Yeah, he built that home, didn't he? Yeah, who? Peekoo. Oh, you had it built.
I knew you had it built. You had it built.
but Auga liked all that, too. His daughter Auga, she likes all that, too. So that's one thing I missed in the hospital.
